subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.stage_label: Observe and question apparent sky motion
periods.activity_title: Shadow Walk and the Moving Sun
periods.activity_description: Students observe Rashmika's puzzle — coconut tree shadows are long in the morning and short at noon — and trace how the Sun's apparent position changes across a day. They sketch a simple diagram of shadow direction and length at three times of day and articulate the question: is the Sun moving, or is something else moving?

roles.role_description: Poses Rashmika's opening puzzle and prompts students to recall any shadow observations they have made themselves.
Sketch shadow diagrams for morning, noon, and evening and write one sentence stating what they think causes the change.

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates Rashmika's observation and asks students whether they have noticed shadows behaving differently at different times of day.
Students individually sketch a top-view diagram showing a vertical stick and its shadow direction and relative length at three times of day, labelling each with the approximate time.
Pairs share their sketches and discuss whether the Sun is moving or the Earth is moving to explain the pattern.
Teacher collects two or three contrasting student explanations on the board as open hypotheses to be tested in subsequent units.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's central puzzle without resolving it, so resist confirming or denying student hypotheses — the goal is to surface what they already believe. Watch for the dominant misconception that the Sun physically travels across the sky; note how many students hold it so you can return to it explicitly in the next unit. Leave the competing hypotheses visible on the board as a reference for what the chapter will address.

periods.stage_label: Observe and question apparent sky motion
periods.activity_description: Using a rotating globe (or a student slowly spinning on a chair) and a fixed torch, students physically experience how a rotating observer sees surrounding objects appear to move in the opposite direction. They record which direction the globe must rotate to produce the observed east-to-west apparent motion of the Sun.

roles.role_description: Sets up the torch as the Sun and demonstrates one slow rotation of the globe, asking students to watch the sticker-marked location pass from dark into light.
Take turns rotating the globe and observing the illuminated and dark halves, then record the rotation direction that produces sunrise in the east.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the competing hypotheses from the previous unit and introduces the merry-go-round analogy from the chapter — when you spin anti-clockwise, surrounding trees appear to spin clockwise.

Groups use a globe with a small sticker marking their city and a torch held steady to represent the Sun; they rotate the globe in both directions and identify which direction makes the sticker move from darkness into torchlight from the east.
Each group records: the direction of rotation (west-to-east), what the illuminated half represents (daytime), and what the dark half represents (nighttime).
Class discussion: students explain in their own words why the Sun appears to rise in the east even though the Sun is stationary — resolving the opening hypothesis.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who built the hypothesis in the previous unit that the Sun moves will now need to reconcile that idea with what they observe here; prompt them with 'What is actually moving in this model?' rather than telling them directly. A common confusion at this stage is that the Earth rotates east-to-west — students may initially spin the globe the wrong way, which is a productive error: ask them what sunrise would look like in that case. Confirm before closing that all groups agree on the west-to-east direction of rotation.

periods.stage_label: Classify and describe Earth's two motions
periods.activity_title: Rotation versus Revolution — Definitions and Evidence
periods.activity_description: Students distinguish rotation (spinning on an axis) from revolution (orbiting another body), attach each definition to the Earth's actual motions, and connect each motion to its observable consequence — the day-night cycle for rotation and the yearly change of visible constellations for revolution.

roles.role_description: Introduces the formal definitions of rotation and revolution, uses a diagram of the Earth's orbit, and narrates the evidence for each motion including the Foucault pendulum and the Aryabhata historical fact.
Complete a two-column comparison table — Rotation vs Revolution — with rows for definition, time to complete one cycle, axis or orbit, and one observable consequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the formal definition of rotation with a diagram of the Earth spinning on its axis, citing the ~24-hour period and Aryabhata's historically precise calculation of 23 hours 56 minutes and 4.1 seconds.

Teacher presents revolution: Earth orbiting the Sun in a nearly circular orbit in approximately 365 days and 6 hours, and explains why facing away from the Sun at night means we see different constellations at different times of year.
Students individually fill in the two-column comparison table, then pair-check their entries with a neighbour.
Teacher draws the table on the board and cold-calls students for each row, correcting any confusion between the two motions.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit formalises what students discovered physically in the previous unit, so anchor the definitions explicitly to what they observed with the globe and torch. The most persistent confusion here is students reversing which motion causes which phenomenon — watch for students writing that revolution causes day and night. The Aryabhata detail is a strong engagement hook: pointing out that a fifth-century scholar computed the rotation period to within four seconds of the modern value tends to generate genuine surprise.
materials: Printed or drawn diagram of Earth's orbit around the Sun

periods.stage_label: Classify and describe Earth's two motions
periods.activity_title: Star Trails and Constellation Calendars — Evidence for Revolution
periods.activity_description: Students examine the chapter's evidence that Earth revolves — star trail photographs showing circular arcs around the Pole Star, and the Bhil and Pawara communities' use of star pattern appearances to predict the monsoon — and classify each piece of evidence as supporting rotation, revolution, or both, with a written justification.

roles.role_description: Presents star trail images and the Bhil-Pawara monsoon-star example from the chapter, then poses the sorting question: which motion does each piece of evidence demonstrate?

Examine the four evidence items — star trails, Pole Star apparent stillness, seasonal constellation change, and Bhil-Pawara monsoon stars — and classify each with a one-sentence justification in a group recording sheet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or describes star trail photographs and explains that the Pole Star appears nearly stationary because the Earth's rotational axis points toward it; other stars leave circular arc trails.
Groups receive a sheet listing four evidence items and classify each as evidence for rotation, revolution, or both, writing one justifying sentence per item.

Groups share their classifications; teacher facilitates discussion on any items where groups disagree, especially seasonal constellation change which students may initially misclassify as rotation evidence.
Teacher consolidates: the Pole Star and star trails are rotation evidence; seasonal constellation change and the Bhil-Pawara monsoon stars are revolution evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: Building directly on the definitions established in the previous unit, this activity asks students to apply those definitions to evaluate real evidence rather than simply recalling them. The most likely error is classifying the nightly movement of stars (rotation) and the seasonal shift in which constellations appear (revolution) as the same phenomenon — probe this by asking whether the star pattern changes from 9 pm to midnight on the same night, versus from March to September. The Bhil and Pawara detail is worth dwelling on briefly as it connects traditional ecological knowledge to the astronomical content.
materials: Printed descriptions or projected images of star trails
Group recording sheets with four evidence items listed

periods.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of seasons
periods.activity_title: Tilted Axis Model — Why Seasons Happen
periods.activity_description: Students use a tilted globe and torch to investigate how the axial tilt concentrates sunlight on the Northern Hemisphere in June and spreads it over a larger area in December, producing summer and winter respectively. They mark the illuminated patch size at two positions and compare intensity.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the orbital positions for June and December with the globe tilted consistently in the same direction, showing how the angle of incoming light changes.

Position the tilted globe at June and December orbital positions relative to the torch, trace the illuminated patch on paper at each position, and compare the patch sizes to infer relative sunlight intensity.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept that the Earth's axis is tilted and remains pointed in the same direction throughout the orbit, using a diagram; connects this to the seasonal question that was left open after understanding revolution.

Groups hold the globe at a fixed tilt and move it to June and December orbital positions relative to the torch; at each position they hold paper against the globe and trace the illuminated patch, then compare patch areas.

Groups record which hemisphere has a smaller, brighter patch (Northern Hemisphere in June = summer) and which has a larger, dimmer patch (Northern Hemisphere in December = winter), and note that Southern Hemisphere has the reverse.
Brief class share-out: teacher confirms the two causal factors — steeper sunlight angle and longer daylight hours — both result from axial tilt.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit addresses the most conceptually demanding part of the seasons content, so the physical model is essential — students who only hear the explanation almost always fall back on the distance misconception. The critical error to watch for is students re-tilting the globe at each orbital position rather than keeping the tilt direction fixed; this changes the geometry entirely and must be caught immediately. Once students have traced the patches, ask them to predict what the equator experiences at both positions — the chapter states the equator always receives about 12 hours of sunlight, which is a strong self-check.

periods.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of seasons
periods.activity_title: Solstices, Equinoxes, and the Distance Misconception
periods.activity_description: Students learn the four special dates of the yearly cycle — summer solstice, winter solstice, spring equinox, autumn equinox — with their Northern Hemisphere calendar dates and day-length signatures. The unit explicitly addresses and refutes the misconception that seasons are caused by Earth–Sun distance variation.

roles.role_description: Presents the four special dates with their day-length characteristics and explains why Earth–Sun distance cannot explain seasons — Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, the Northern Hemisphere's winter.
Annotate a pre-drawn orbital diagram with the four dates, their day-length descriptions, and the label 'Northern Hemisphere summer' or 'winter' at each position.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the summer solstice (~21 June, longest day), winter solstice (~22 December, shortest day), and the two equinoxes (~21 March and ~23 September, each with 12 hours of daylight) in the Northern Hemisphere, connecting each to the tilted-globe model from the previous unit.

Teacher explicitly addresses the distance misconception: if distance caused seasons, Northern Hemisphere should have summer when Earth is nearest the Sun — but Earth is nearest in January, which is Northern Hemisphere winter. Students note this refutation.

Students annotate a pre-drawn orbital diagram with the four special dates, their day-length descriptions, and whether the Northern Hemisphere is in summer, winter, or equal-day conditions at each position.
Teacher cold-calls students to explain what happens at the polar regions — six months of daylight followed by six months of darkness — as an extreme consequence of the same axial tilt mechanism.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the tilted-axis model from the previous unit and consolidates the causal explanation by adding the specific calendar markers and tackling misconceptions head-on. The distance misconception is explicitly addressed in the chapter's Dive Deeper box and is worth spending time on — the key counter-evidence is that Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, which is a striking and memorable fact. Students annotating the orbital diagram is a productive check: if a student places summer at the nearest-to-Sun position, the misconception has not been resolved.
homework: Sketch the orbital diagram from memory and label all four special dates with their approximate calendar date, the Northern Hemisphere season, and whether the day is longer or shorter than 12 hours.

periods.stage_label: Explain the geometry and conditions of eclipses
periods.activity_title: Apparent Size and the Solar Eclipse Geometry
periods.activity_description: The teacher demonstrates apparent size using a small disc and a large disc at different distances, then students use a thumb-and-friend activity from the chapter to experience how a small close object can completely cover a large far object. They then apply this principle to explain why the Moon can block the Sun during a solar eclipse.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates apparent size with two discs at different distances, then explains the geometry of a solar eclipse — Moon between Sun and Earth — using a diagram showing the shadow cone falling on a small part of Earth's surface.
Perform the thumb-covers-friend's-head activity from the chapter, then sketch the solar eclipse geometry showing the Moon's shadow cone and label the total and partial eclipse zones.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates apparent size by holding a 2 cm disc close to one eye and a 20 cm disc at a distance, showing they can appear the same size, then explains that the Moon and Sun have nearly equal apparent sizes for an observer on Earth.
Students do the thumb-covers-friend's-head activity: outstretched thumb covers a friend's head at arm's length, demonstrating that a smaller closer object can completely block a larger far one.

Teacher draws the solar eclipse geometry on the board — Sun, Moon, Earth in line with the Moon's shadow cone — and students copy and annotate the diagram, labelling the zone of total solar eclipse and the surrounding zone of partial solar eclipse.

Teacher explains the safety caution from the chapter — direct viewing causes permanent blindness — and the transit of Venus example showing why Mercury and Venus cannot cause a solar eclipse despite being larger than the Moon.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit introduces eclipse geometry, which connects directly to the revolutionary and positional knowledge built across the earlier units — eclipses occur because of specific alignments of Earth, Moon, and Sun during their orbital motions. The most common misconception is that any new Moon produces a solar eclipse; the chapter does not cover the Moon's inclined orbit explicitly, but you can note that alignments are rare without introducing new geometry. Emphasise the safety warning with genuine emphasis — the chapter is explicit that even sunglasses are insufficient protection.
materials: Small disc (~2 cm) and large disc (~20 cm) for demonstration

periods.stage_label: Explain the geometry and conditions of eclipses
periods.activity_title: Lunar Eclipse Geometry and the Red Moon
periods.activity_description: Students investigate the geometry of a lunar eclipse — Earth between Sun and Moon — by constructing a shadow diagram and explaining why the fully eclipsed Moon appears dark red rather than disappearing completely. They compare the geometry and observability conditions of solar and lunar eclipses.

roles.role_description: Poses the question of why the Moon turns red during a total lunar eclipse rather than going completely dark, and guides students to the role of Earth's atmosphere in refracting sunlight.

Construct the lunar eclipse geometry diagram showing Sun, Earth, Moon alignment, annotate the Earth's shadow zone, and answer the inquiry question about the red colour using the atmosphere-refraction explanation from the chapter.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the opening inquiry: in a lunar eclipse the Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon — so why does the Moon turn red rather than going completely black?
Groups construct the lunar eclipse diagram — Sun, Earth, Moon in alignment with the Earth's shadow cone falling on the Moon — and annotate the zones of total and partial lunar eclipse.

Groups discuss and write a one-paragraph answer to the red Moon question using the chapter's explanation: some sunlight is refracted through Earth's atmosphere and reaches the Moon, giving it a dark red appearance.

Class comparison of solar and lunar eclipse diagrams: students identify the key geometric difference (which body is in the middle) and the key observability difference (lunar eclipses are safe to view with the naked eye; solar eclipses are not).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit pairs naturally with the previous unit on solar eclipses — students now have both eclipse geometries and can compare them directly. The red Moon explanation is often surprising to students; it connects to the idea that Earth's atmosphere bends light, which is a concept they may encounter more formally in later study, so present it as an intriguing consequence rather than a detailed optical derivation. A useful checkpoint: ask each group to state in one sentence what is in the middle for each eclipse type — this reveals whether the geometry is secure before the unit closes.
materials: Coloured pencils (red for shadow zone annotation)
homework: Draw both eclipse diagrams from memory — solar and lunar — and write one sentence under each explaining which body is in the middle and one sentence explaining the safe viewing condition for each.

periods.stage_label: Apply relative positions and motions to predict and explain phenomena
periods.activity_title: Predicting Sky Phenomena from Orbital Position
periods.activity_description: Students are given four orbital scenario cards — each describing a specific alignment or position of Earth, Moon, and Sun — and must predict the observable sky phenomenon that results, explaining which motion or positional condition causes it. Scenarios draw on all chapter content: day-night, seasons, and eclipses.

roles.role_description: Distributes the scenario cards and models the prediction-and-explanation format for the first scenario, then circulates to probe group reasoning.
For each scenario card, write the predicted observable phenomenon and a causal explanation linking it to the specific orbital motion or alignment described.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the task: each scenario card describes a position or alignment, and groups must name the phenomenon and give the causal mechanism — the format models scientific prediction from positional data.

Groups work through four scenario cards: (1) Northern Hemisphere tilted toward Sun with day longer than 12 hours; (2) Earth's shadow falling entirely on the Moon; (3) Moon positioned between Sun and Earth, shadows falling on a small region; (4) location on Earth rotating into sunlight from the west-to-east direction.
Groups exchange cards and peer-assess one another's explanations, checking that each explanation names the relevant motion (rotation, revolution, orbital alignment) as the cause.
Teacher highlights any explanations where cause and phenomenon were reversed or confused, setting up the final unit's consolidation work.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the first in the final stage and deliberately crosses all three content domains — rotation, revolution/seasons, eclipses — to test whether students can identify which motion explains which phenomenon without being told which category the question belongs to. The most diagnostic error to watch for is students explaining seasonal phenomena with eclipse language or vice versa, which indicates the categories are not yet integrated. The peer-assessment step is deliberate: explaining why another group's answer is incomplete requires a higher level of engagement than producing one's own answer.
materials: Four scenario cards (pre-prepared by teacher, one set per group)

periods.stage_label: Apply relative positions and motions to predict and explain phenomena
periods.activity_title: Eclipse Prediction and the Significance of Orbital Motion
periods.activity_description: Students examine how knowledge of Earth, Moon, and Sun positions enables prediction of eclipses and seasonal phenomena — including the ancient Indian astronomical texts and the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory — and evaluate a set of claims about celestial phenomena by applying the causal explanations built across the chapter.

roles.role_description: Facilitates a structured discussion in which students evaluate three claims about celestial phenomena, drawing on the full chapter's causal framework and referencing the historical and contemporary significance of eclipse prediction.
Evaluate three written claims — one correct, one containing the distance-causes-seasons misconception, one reversing the eclipse geometry — explaining whether each is correct or flawed and why.
Share and debate their individual evaluations, reaching a group consensus explanation for each claim that they can defend to the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects to the scenario prediction work from the previous unit and introduces the broader significance: eclipse prediction from Surya Siddhanta to the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory demonstrates that understanding orbital positions has practical and cultural importance.

Students individually evaluate three written claims: Claim A — 'Northern India is cold in December because the Earth is farthest from the Sun then'; Claim B — 'During a total lunar eclipse the Moon disappears completely because no light reaches it'; Claim C — 'The Sun appears to rise in the east because Earth rotates from west to east'. Each student writes whether the claim is correct or flawed and why.
Groups discuss and consolidate their evaluations, resolving disagreements using the causal explanations from the chapter — the group must produce a single corrected version of each flawed claim.

Teacher takes whole-class responses: Claim A is flawed (distance does not cause seasons; axial tilt does, and Earth is closest to Sun in January); Claim B is flawed (the Moon turns red, not invisible, due to atmospheric refraction); Claim C is correct. Chapter is closed.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit brings together the three causal mechanisms built across the chapter by asking students to evaluate claims rather than simply produce explanations — a higher-order operation that the previous unit's scenario work has prepared them for. Both flawed claims correspond to misconceptions explicitly addressed in the chapter's Dive Deeper boxes, so students have the chapter evidence available to them. Watch for students who correctly identify a claim as flawed but give an incomplete correction — the correction itself, not just the identification, is the measure of whether the causal understanding is secure.
materials: Printed or board-written claim cards (three claims)

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and question apparent sky motion
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe and sketch the apparent daily movement of the Sun's shadow, then use a rotating globe and torch to experience how the Earth's west-to-east rotation produces the Sun's apparent east-to-west motion.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the apparent daily motion of the Sun across the sky and demonstrate, using a rotating globe model, that this motion is caused by the Earth's west-to-east rotation rather than by the Sun's own movement.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and describe Earth's two motions
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students formally distinguish rotation from revolution, complete a comparison table of their defining characteristics, and classify star trail and seasonal constellation evidence as supporting one or both motions.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can distinguish Earth's rotation from its revolution by their definitions, periods, and observable consequences, and correctly classify given evidence — including star trails, Pole Star apparent stillness, and seasonal constellation changes — as supporting rotation, revolution, or both.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of seasons
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use a tilted globe and torch to investigate how axial tilt concentrates or spreads sunlight across hemispheres, then annotate an orbital diagram with the four special dates and explicitly refute the distance-causes-seasons misconception.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why axial tilt — not Earth–Sun distance — causes seasons, identify the summer solstice, winter solstice, and equinoxes on an orbital diagram by their day-length signatures, and state why the Northern Hemisphere is colder in January despite the Earth being nearest the Sun at that time.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain the geometry and conditions of eclipses
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use apparent-size demonstrations and geometry diagrams to explain how the Moon blocks the Sun in a solar eclipse and how Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse, comparing the geometry, observability conditions, and the red-Moon phenomenon.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct geometry diagrams for both solar and lunar eclipses, label the body in the middle and the shadow zones for each, explain why the Moon can cover the Sun despite being smaller, and explain why the fully eclipsed Moon appears red rather than disappearing completely.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply relative positions and motions to predict and explain phenomena
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students predict and justify observable sky phenomena from orbital scenario descriptions, then evaluate flawed and correct claims about celestial phenomena by applying the causal explanations for rotation, seasons, and eclipses built across the chapter.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can apply their understanding of the relative positions and motions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun to predict the phenomenon produced by a given orbital scenario and to evaluate written claims about celestial phenomena — identifying flawed causal reasoning and producing corrected explanations.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and question apparent sky motion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the apparent daily motion of the Sun across the sky and demonstrate, using a rotating globe model, that this motion is caused by the Earth's west-to-east rotation rather than by the Sun's own movement.

competency.competency_text: Observing and identifying celestial objects and explaining their role in navigation, calendars, and other phenomena including phases of the moon and eclipses.

assessment_items.question_text: Rashmika observes that the Sun appears to rise in the east, move across the sky, and set in the west every day. What is the correct explanation for this apparent motion?

options.label: A
options.text: The Earth revolves around the Sun from east to west, causing the Sun to appear to rise and set each day.

options.label: B
options.text: The Earth rotates from east to west on its own axis, which pushes the Sun in the opposite direction.

options.label: C
options.text: The Earth rotates from west to east on its own axis, making the Sun appear to move from east to west.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun revolves around the Earth from east to west, completing one revolution in 24 hours.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student holds the classic misconception that the Sun physically moves around the Earth; they have not shifted from the everyday observational frame to a heliocentric model.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly identifies Earth's rotation as the cause but has the direction reversed — a common confusion between the direction of rotation and the direction of apparent motion that the globe-and-torch activity was designed to address.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates rotation with revolution and attributes the daily cycle to Earth's yearly orbital motion rather than its daily spin.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract direction language (west-to-east vs east-to-west) can be invited to mime the merry-go-round analogy from the chapter — spinning themselves slowly and watching which way a fixed object appears to move — before re-reading the options.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and question apparent sky motion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the apparent daily motion of the Sun across the sky and demonstrate, using a rotating globe model, that this motion is caused by the Earth's west-to-east rotation rather than by the Sun's own movement.

competency.competency_text: Observing and identifying celestial objects and explaining their role in navigation, calendars, and other phenomena including phases of the moon and eclipses.

assessment_items.question_text: In the globe-and-torch model of day and night, a sticker marks a city on the globe. When the globe is rotated from west to east, what does the sticker's movement from the dark side into the torchlight represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The city completing one full revolution around the Sun.

options.label: B
options.text: The city experiencing sunrise as the Earth's rotation brings it into sunlight.

options.label: C
options.text: The city experiencing sunset as it moves away from the Sun's light.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun moving eastward to illuminate a new part of Earth.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has confused the direction of movement — they know rotation causes day and night but have the sunrise-sunset mapping backwards, likely because they reversed the rotation direction mentally.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has not fully released the misconception that the Sun moves; they interpret the model's torchlight as something that shifts rather than the globe as the moving component.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused rotation (daily spin) with revolution (yearly orbit) — a category confusion that the comparison table in Stage 2 was designed to address.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the spatial reasoning challenging can physically enact the model — one student holds the torch still while another slowly rotates holding a globe or a ball with a sticker — before answering.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and describe Earth's two motions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can distinguish Earth's rotation from its revolution by their definitions, periods, and observable consequences, and correctly classify given evidence — including star trails, Pole Star apparent stillness, and seasonal constellation changes — as supporting rotation, revolution, or both.

competency.competency_text: Observing and identifying celestial objects and explaining their role in navigation, calendars, and other phenomena including phases of the moon and eclipses.

assessment_items.question_text: An astrophotographer keeps a camera shutter open for several hours at night, pointing at the northern sky. The resulting photograph shows circular arc trails for most stars, while one star appears as a single bright dot with almost no arc. Which statement correctly explains both observations?

options.label: A
options.text: All stars move at different speeds around the Earth; the dot-star moves slowest.

options.label: B
options.text: The Earth revolves around the Sun; the Pole Star is in the direction of Earth's orbit so it stays fixed while other stars shift.

options.label: C
options.text: The Earth rotates, causing all stars including the Pole Star to trace equal circular arcs; the dot appearance is due to the star being much dimmer.

options.label: D
options.text: The Earth rotates on its axis; the arc-stars appear to circle the Pole Star, which lies almost exactly along Earth's rotational axis and so appears nearly stationary.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student attributes differential star motion to intrinsic star speeds rather than to the geometry of Earth's axis — a misconception that bypasses the rotation explanation entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly identifies the Pole Star as special but misattributes the phenomenon to revolution rather than rotation — a confusion between the two motions that the classification activity was designed to resolve.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies Earth's rotation as the cause of star trails but fails to apply the axis-direction principle and instead invokes an unrelated property (dimness) to explain the Pole Star's appearance.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be asked to first decide: does the photograph show something that changes over one night, or over many months? That question routes them to rotation as the relevant motion before they evaluate the options.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and describe Earth's two motions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can distinguish Earth's rotation from its revolution by their definitions, periods, and observable consequences, and correctly classify given evidence — including star trails, Pole Star apparent stillness, and seasonal constellation changes — as supporting rotation, revolution, or both.

competency.competency_text: Observing and identifying celestial objects and explaining their role in navigation, calendars, and other phenomena including phases of the moon and eclipses.

assessment_items.question_text: The Bhil and Pawara communities of the Tapi Valley traditionally observed the appearance of specific star patterns in the night sky to predict the approaching monsoon season. Which of Earth's motions makes this observation reliable year after year?

options.label: A
options.text: Earth's revolution around the Sun, because as Earth orbits, the portion of sky visible at night changes predictably through the year.

options.label: B
options.text: Earth's rotation, because it brings different constellations into the night sky over the course of a single night.

options.label: C
options.text: Earth's rotation, because the 24-hour spin cycle aligns star positions with the monsoon calendar.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon's revolution around Earth, because the Moon's monthly cycle marks the seasonal calendar used by these communities.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student knows rotation changes the visible sky but does not distinguish between the nightly change (rotation) and the yearly seasonal change (revolution) — the most common confusion between these two motions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Same rotation-revolution confusion as option A, with an additional invented mechanism (24-hour cycle aligning with monsoon calendar) that reveals the student is conflating timescales.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student substitutes the Moon's revolution for Earth's revolution — an error that reveals incomplete understanding of which orbital motion produces year-long seasonal cycles.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be prompted to consider the timescale: does the monsoon come at the same time each day, or the same time each year? This routes them to identify the yearly motion (revolution) as the relevant one.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and describe Earth's two motions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can distinguish Earth's rotation from its revolution by their definitions, periods, and observable consequences, and correctly classify given evidence — including star trails, Pole Star apparent stillness, and seasonal constellation changes — as supporting rotation, revolution, or both.

competency.competency_text: Observing and identifying celestial objects and explaining their role in navigation, calendars, and other phenomena including phases of the moon and eclipses.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'The Big Dipper (Saptarishi) constellation appears to move across the sky during one night, and it also appears in a different position in the sky in March compared to September. Both movements are caused by the same motion of the Earth.' Is the student correct? Explain your answer by naming the Earth motion responsible for each observation.
expected_elements: The student's claim is incorrect — the two movements are caused by different Earth motions.
The nightly movement of the Big Dipper across the sky during a single night is caused by Earth's rotation on its axis (approximately 24-hour cycle).

The difference in the constellation's position between March and September is caused by Earth's revolution around the Sun (approximately 365-day cycle), which changes the portion of the sky facing away from the Sun at night.
These are two distinct motions with different timescales and different observable consequences.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find written explanation difficult can first draw a quick two-row table (rotation vs revolution) and fill in 'timescale' and 'observation' columns before writing their answer as prose.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism of seasons
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why axial tilt — not Earth–Sun distance — causes seasons, identify the summer solstice, winter solstice, and equinoxes on an orbital diagram by their day-length signatures, and state why the Northern Hemisphere is colder in January despite the Earth being nearest the Sun at that time.

competency.competency_text: Observing and identifying celestial objects and explaining their role in navigation, calendars, and other phenomena including phases of the moon and eclipses.

assessment_items.question_text: In June, the Northern Hemisphere experiences summer, with long days and high temperatures. Which combination of conditions, both caused by axial tilt, directly produces these higher temperatures?

options.label: A
options.text: Sunlight strikes the Northern Hemisphere at a steeper angle, concentrating energy over a smaller area, and the Northern Hemisphere receives more than 12 hours of daylight per day.

options.label: B
options.text: Sunlight strikes the Northern Hemisphere at a steeper angle only; day length remains 12 hours throughout the year because Earth's rotation period does not change.

options.label: C
options.text: The Northern Hemisphere is physically closer to the Sun in June, and this shorter distance increases the Sun's intensity.

options.label: D
options.text: The Northern Hemisphere receives more than 12 hours of daylight only; the angle of sunlight does not change because Earth's axis is always perpendicular to its orbit.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student holds the distance-causes-seasons misconception that is explicitly addressed in the chapter's Dive Deeper box — they have not integrated the axial tilt explanation as the replacement.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student partially understands axial tilt (steeper angle) but incorrectly holds that day length is constant — they have not connected the tilt to the variation in daylight hours across the year.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student partially understands the daylight-hours effect but denies the angle effect and additionally holds the misconception that Earth's axis is perpendicular to its orbit (untilted) — a direct contradiction of the chapter's core content.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can refer to the tilted-globe traced patches from the activity: if the patch was smaller in June, that means energy is concentrated — both the concentration and the duration are features of the same tilted geometry.

assessment_items.question_text: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, yet January is winter in the Northern Hemisphere. Which statement best explains this apparent contradiction?

options.label: A
options.text: Earth moves faster along its orbit in January, so the Northern Hemisphere receives less total sunlight even though it is closer.

options.label: B
options.text: In January, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun — sunlight strikes at a shallower angle and days are shorter than 12 hours — so temperature is lower despite the shorter Earth–Sun distance.

options.label: C
options.text: The difference in Earth–Sun distance between January and July is large enough to reverse the effect of axial tilt, making January colder despite the tilt factor.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun emits less energy in January, which coincides with Earth being closest to it, reducing the heat received by the Northern Hemisphere.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student invents an orbital-speed mechanism not in the chapter — they sense that distance alone cannot explain the contradiction but lack the axial tilt explanation to replace it.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student attributes seasonal temperature change to variation in the Sun's energy output — an external factor not discussed in the chapter and a sign that the tilt-based causal chain has not been internalised.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student acknowledges axial tilt but reverses the chapter's point — the chapter explicitly states that the distance difference is too small to reverse the tilt effect, and this option inverts that relationship.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be guided to recall the traced patch sizes from the tilted-globe activity: in January the Northern Hemisphere patch is large and dim — that visual memory anchors the tilt explanation independent of the distance fact.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Orbital position | Approximate date | Northern Hemisphere day length | Northern Hemisphere season
P | ~21 June | Longest day of the year | ?
Q | ~23 September | Exactly 12 hours | ?
R | ~22 December | Shortest day of the year | ?

assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Complete the Northern Hemisphere season column for positions P, Q, R, and S. Then select one of the four positions and explain, in terms of axial tilt and sunlight angle, why the Northern Hemisphere has the season you named.
expected_elements: P (~21 June): Summer (summer solstice — longest day, Northern Hemisphere tilted toward Sun).
Q (~23 September): Autumn equinox — equal day and night; neither hemisphere tilted more toward the Sun.
R (~22 December): Winter (winter solstice — shortest day, Northern Hemisphere tilted away from Sun).
S (~21 March): Spring equinox — equal day and night.

For the chosen position, explanation includes reference to axial tilt direction (toward or away from Sun) and its effect on sunlight angle (steep = concentrated = warmer, or shallow = spread = cooler).

assessment_items.question_text: During a total solar eclipse, the Moon completely covers the Sun as seen from a small region on Earth. The Moon's diameter is about 400 times smaller than the Sun's. Which principle explains how the Moon can completely block the Sun despite being so much smaller?

options.label: A
options.text: Apparent size depends on both actual size and distance; the Moon is about 400 times closer to Earth than the Sun, so their apparent sizes as seen from Earth are nearly equal.

options.label: B
options.text: The Moon expands slightly as it passes in front of the Sun due to heat from solar radiation.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon is denser than the Sun, which allows it to absorb all sunlight and appear larger than its actual size.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun's light bends around the Moon due to refraction, making the Moon appear large enough to cover the Sun completely.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has not engaged with the apparent-size principle and instead invents a physical change in the Moon — they lack the conceptual tool to explain the size discrepancy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates density with apparent size — a confusion between physical properties and observational geometry that the thumb-covers-head activity was designed to address.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student misapplies refraction (a concept relevant to the lunar eclipse red-colour explanation) to the solar eclipse situation, revealing a confusion between the two eclipse phenomena.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can revisit the thumb-covers-friend's-head activity mentally: the thumb is smaller than a head but covers it at arm's length — the same distance-governs-apparent-size principle applies to the Moon and Sun.

assessment_items.question_text: During a total lunar eclipse, observers on Earth see the Moon turn dark red rather than disappearing completely. What causes this red colour?

options.label: A
options.text: Red light from nearby stars is reflected off the Moon's surface when the Sun's white light is blocked.

options.label: B
options.text: The Moon heats up as it enters Earth's shadow, causing its surface rocks to glow red from stored heat.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon passes through the red light emitted by the Sun's corona during the eclipse, giving it a red tint.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon's surface reflects the red light of sunsets and sunrises occurring around the edge of the Earth, as some sunlight is refracted through Earth's atmosphere and reaches the Moon.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student attributes the red colour to thermal emission from the Moon — a misconception that confuses light emission with light reflection and ignores the atmosphere-refraction explanation from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student misplaces the source of red light to the Sun's corona rather than to Earth's atmosphere — a confusion between solar and terrestrial optical phenomena.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly identifies that ordinary sunlight is blocked but invents an unrelated light source (nearby stars) rather than applying the atmospheric refraction principle from the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can think about what we see at sunrise and sunset (reddish light due to Earth's atmosphere) and then apply the same principle to light bending around Earth's edge toward the Moon.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'A solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse are basically the same event — in both cases the Moon blocks the Sun.' Identify the error in this claim and explain the correct geometry for each type of eclipse, including which body occupies the middle position.
expected_elements: The claim is incorrect: in a lunar eclipse, the Moon does not block the Sun.
In a solar eclipse, the Moon is in the middle — positioned between the Sun and Earth — and its shadow falls on part of Earth's surface.
In a lunar eclipse, the Earth is in the middle — positioned between the Sun and the Moon — and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
The student has confused which body is in the middle position in each case.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find prose explanation difficult can draw two simple diagrams — one for each eclipse type — labelling the order of the three bodies and the direction the shadow falls, and then write one sentence per diagram instead of a continuous paragraph.

assessment_items.question_text: An observer in the Northern Hemisphere notices it is midday and the sky has gone unexpectedly dark for a few minutes. The Moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun. Which phenomenon is occurring, and what orbital condition makes this event rare rather than happening every month?

options.label: A
options.text: A partial solar eclipse is occurring; the Moon covers the Sun partially every month at new Moon but most observers do not notice the slight dimming.

options.label: B
options.text: A total lunar eclipse is occurring; it is rare because the Earth's shadow is small and the Moon only enters it occasionally.

options.label: C
options.text: A total solar eclipse is occurring; it is rare because the Moon is only close enough to Earth to cover the Sun once every few years.

options.label: D
options.text: A total solar eclipse is occurring; it is rare because the Moon's orbital plane is slightly tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane, so perfect alignment does not occur every month.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly identifies the rarity condition logic but misidentifies the phenomenon — they have confused which body is in the middle, indicating the eclipse geometry is not secure.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies the solar eclipse but invents a distance-based rarity mechanism not in the chapter — they have not connected rarity to orbital plane inclination.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student partially understands solar eclipse geometry but misidentifies the regularity — claiming it happens monthly reveals they have not registered that orbital alignment is the rarity condition.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students unsure of the rarity reason can consider: if the Moon's orbit were in exactly the same plane as Earth's orbit, what would happen at every new Moon? This counterfactual routes them to identify plane tilt as the key condition.

assessment_items.question_text: A student writes: 'Regions near the equator in southern India experience more extreme seasons than regions in northern India, because the equator is closer to the Sun.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from the chapter.

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct — the equator is closer to the Sun and receives more direct sunlight, producing stronger seasonal temperature swings.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is correct — the equator receives the most intense sunlight year-round, which creates large temperature differences between summer and winter.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is incorrect — southern India experiences more extreme seasons because it is in the Southern Hemisphere, which has opposite seasons to the Northern Hemisphere.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is incorrect — the equator always receives approximately 12 hours of sunlight regardless of Earth's orbital position, so the effect of seasons is minimal there; seasonal variation is stronger at higher latitudes like northern India.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student accepts the distance premise (equator closer to Sun) without questioning it and extends it incorrectly — they have not applied the axial-tilt explanation to understand why the equator's day length is constant.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly rejects the claim but gives an incorrect reason — placing southern India in the Southern Hemisphere, which contradicts geographic knowledge and the chapter's reference to southern India as a region near the equator.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student correctly identifies that the equator receives intense sunlight but reverses the conclusion — high year-round intensity means minimal seasonal variation, not extreme swings.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can anchor their evaluation to the orbital diagram they annotated: at both June and December positions, what does the chapter say about the equator's day length? That single fact (always ~12 hours) is sufficient to evaluate the claim.

assessment_items.question_text: Ancient Indian astronomers, including the authors of the Surya Siddhanta, were able to predict solar and lunar eclipses with precision long before modern telescopes existed. Using what you have learned about the motions of Earth, Moon, and Sun, explain what knowledge of orbital positions these astronomers must have possessed, and why accurate prediction of eclipses required understanding more than one type of celestial motion.
look_for: Student identifies that eclipse prediction requires knowing the orbital motion of the Moon around Earth and of Earth (and Moon) around the Sun simultaneously.

Student explains that a solar eclipse requires Sun-Moon-Earth alignment (Moon between Sun and Earth) and a lunar eclipse requires Sun-Earth-Moon alignment (Earth between Sun and Moon) — showing they can distinguish the two geometries in this applied context.
Student articulates why multiple motions must be tracked: the Moon orbits Earth while Earth orbits the Sun, so both cycles must be known to predict when all three bodies will align.

Student connects the precision of ancient predictions (as referenced in the chapter's Fascinating Facts box on Surya Siddhanta) to the sophistication of this multi-motion knowledge — not treating prediction as guesswork.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the open writing format daunting can be invited to first list the two types of eclipse and the body in the middle for each, then separately list the two orbital motions involved, before connecting them in prose — this scaffolds the integration without providing the answer.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Description of observation | Phenomenon occurring | Earth motion(s) responsible | Causal explanation
1 | It is midday in Chennai and the sky turns dark for several minutes; the Moon is directly between the Sun and Earth. | | | 
2 | In December, a school in Shimla (Northern India) records only 9 hours of daylight; a school near Kochi (close to the equator) records nearly 12 hours on the same day. | | | 
3 | A photographer in Jaipur keeps a camera pointing at the northern sky for 4 hours and photographs circular star arcs; the Pole Star shows almost no arc. | | |

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each of the four scenarios, identify the phenomenon occurring, name the Earth motion or motions responsible, and write a causal explanation connecting the described observation to the relevant orbital geometry.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each row: (1) name the phenomenon; (2) name the Earth motion(s) involved — rotation, revolution, Moon's revolution around Earth, or a combination; (3) write one or two sentences explaining why the described observation occurs, using the positions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.
format_of_output: Completed table with all four rows filled in
Each explanation row must be in the student's own words — not copied from the scenario description

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A scenario table requires students to read a structured description of an observation, identify the phenomenon, and supply a causal explanation — this is the most direct demonstration vehicle for the final stage LO, which requires applying positional and motion knowledge to predict and explain phenomena across all three content domains of the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can integrate knowledge of rotation, revolution, and eclipse geometry — reading a described observation and identifying both the phenomenon and the causal chain without being told which domain the question belongs to.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-column scaffold (phenomenon, motion responsible, causal explanation) separates identification from classification from explanation, making it diagnostic: a student who names the phenomenon correctly but gives the wrong motion has a classification gap; a student who names the correct motion but gives a circular explanation has a causal reasoning gap.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name the specific phenomenon (e.g. total solar eclipse, winter solstice condition, star trail due to rotation, total lunar eclipse), identify the correct motion or alignment, and give a causal sentence that references positions or geometry (e.g. 'Earth is between Sun and Moon so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon'). Weak responses name a phenomenon but give a definition rather than an explanation, or give the correct phenomenon for one scenario while applying the wrong motion category.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write the explanation in prose can sketch a small diagram in the explanation cell showing the positions of the relevant bodies — the diagram itself demonstrates causal understanding and can be accepted as equivalent evidence.
